query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a nominally single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy, toughness degradation after intermediate-temperature exposure arises primarily from the emergence of nanoscale chemical short-range order (SRO) clusters within the grains, which locally reduce the stacking-fault energy, promote highly planar slip and strain localization, and thereby trigger premature micro-crack initiation—without the need for grain-boundary segregation or second-phase precipitation that dominate embrittlement in conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Solution-annealed, fully recrystallised, equiatomic Co–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ni (‘Cantor’) alloy with ~10 µm equiaxed grains, single-phase FCC, no detectable SRO or second phases.
generation.intervention: Isothermal ageing at 500 °C for 100 h in vacuum (or inert atmosphere) followed by water quench, chosen to maximise SRO formation while minimising long-range ordering or intermetallic precipitation.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing at 25 °C under high strain-rate impact (Charpy V-notch) and quasi-static tension; microstructural characterisation by high-energy XRD, HRTEM and atom-probe tomography on both as-annealed (baseline) and aged conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanometre-scale Cr/Mn-enriched SRO clusters dispersed within grains; no measurable grain-boundary segregation or precipitate formation.
generation.mechanism: SRO clusters locally lower the stacking-fault energy, forcing dislocations to glide on coplanar {111} planes with limited cross-slip. The resulting concentrated slip bands elevate local stress triaxiality, nucleate micro-voids at SRO–matrix interfaces and promote intergranular micro-crack linkage, reducing absorbed impact energy long before any grain-boundary precipitation occurs.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the unaged baseline, 500 °C/100 h exposure will (i) reduce room-temperature Charpy impact energy by at least 40 ± 15 %, (ii) shorten uniform tensile elongation by ~30 %, (iii) leave yield strength nearly unchanged (±5 %), and (iv) show fracture surfaces containing facets that initiate inside grains rather than along boundaries. Grain boundaries will remain chemically homogeneous, whereas bulk APT/TEM will reveal a measurable Warren–Cowley SRO parameter (|α| > 0.05 at r ≈ 0.3–1 nm), absent in the baseline.
generation.baseline: As-annealed, unaged alloy tested under identical loading and temperature, exhibiting high Charpy energy (>200 J cm⁻²) and >55 % total elongation with homogeneous ductile fracture.
generation.boundary: Effect expected for ageing temperatures 400–600 °C and times >10 h; negligible below 300 °C (insufficient atomic mobility) and above ~800 °C (SRO dissolves). Applies to FCC, medium-to-high SFE HEAs of similar composition; not expected in BCC refractory HEAs where SRO chemistry and slip behaviour differ.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of SRO-induced SFE reduction is estimated from CALPHAD/DFT but not yet directly measured; possible concurrent vacancy clustering or undetected clusters (<1 nm) could contribute; precise toughness drop may vary with grain size and impurity level.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three specimen sets from the same heat: (A) baseline (no ageing); (B) aged 500 °C/100 h; (C) aged 800 °C/100 h. Confirm by APT and TEM that (B) contains SRO clusters without grain-boundary segregation or precipitates, (C) shows neither. Measure Charpy impact energy and tensile properties at 25 °C for all sets.
measurements: Yield strength and uniform elongation from tensile tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if brittle-like toughness loss (>20 % reduction in Charpy energy) is observed only when grain-boundary segregation or precipitates are present, or if set (B) shows no significant toughness loss despite confirmed intragranular SRO, or if set (C) (lacking SRO) still shows equivalent embrittlement. Either outcome would indicate that SRO is not the primary driver of toughness degradation.
